Chapter 7: Resisting Social Pressure and Building Resilience
As kids grow up, they start to feel more and more pressure to fit in—whether it’s coming from friends, what they see on TV, or even the rules at school. Sometimes that pressure is obvious, but other times, it’s really subtle. And more often than not, it pushes them toward traditional gender roles and expectations.
So, how do we help children recognize these influences and learn to stand up to them? Well, teaching them to resist social pressure is a big part of raising them with feminist values.
Resilience really starts with self-awareness. When a child understands their own values and boundaries, they’re way better equipped to handle outside pressures. One of the most powerful things you can do as a caregiver is to keep those lines of communication open—don’t shy away from tough conversations about things like peer pressure, bullying, or feeling left out.
Try asking questions like, “How did that make you feel?” or “What do you think is the right thing to do?” These simple questions help kids pause and reflect, so they can start building their own sense of right and wrong.
There are some really practical ways to build resilience, too. For example, you can role-play situations where your child might feel pressured to go along with the crowd, and together, brainstorm different ways they could respond. Or, help them put words to their feelings—when kids can name what they’re experiencing, it’s a lot easier for them to respond thoughtfully, instead of just reacting in the moment.
And don’t forget about friendships. Encourage your child to spend time with peers who share their values—friends who truly support their individuality make a huge difference.
But let’s be honest—resisting social pressure isn’t always easy. Sometimes, it feels lonely. Kids might worry about being left out, or misunderstood, just because they’re choosing to do what feels right. That’s where you come in: share your own stories about standing up for what you believe in, and let your child know their feelings are real and valid.
Here’s something important: resilience doesn’t mean your child will never feel hurt or discouraged. It means they learn how to bounce back—even when things are tough. When you normalize setbacks and talk about the importance of self-care, you’re helping your child build the kind of inner strength they’ll carry with them for life.
So, the real takeaway here? By teaching kids to recognize social pressure, supporting them as they resist it, and helping them recover from setbacks, you’re setting them up to navigate a complicated world with confidence and compassion.
